title: Crystal Structures
description: Twelve original questions on lattices, bases, cubic structures, packing, crystallographic directions and X-ray diffraction. Multiple-response items use the announced Quiz 1 scoring: +1 per correct selection, -0.5 per incorrect selection, floored at zero. Includes planar density, multi-species density assumptions and XRD geometry.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly describe the lattice-and-basis description of a crystal?

options.content: A lattice is a periodic array of equivalent points.
A basis must contain exactly one atom.
The same basis is attached to every lattice point.
Every lattice point is itself a physical atom.

questions.explanation: A crystal structure is generated by placing an identical basis at each point of a periodic lattice. The basis may contain one atom or a group of atoms, while a lattice point is a mathematical location rather than necessarily an atom.

questions.prompt: A monatomic FCC crystal has lattice constant $a=0.40\ \mathrm{nm}$. What is the planar atomic density of its (100) plane? Count atom centres on that plane.

options.content: $6.25\ \mathrm{atoms}\,\mathrm{nm}^{-2}$
$25.0\ \mathrm{atoms}\,\mathrm{nm}^{-2}$
$12.5\ \mathrm{atoms}\,\mathrm{nm}^{-2}$
$62.5\ \mathrm{atoms}\,\mathrm{nm}^{-2}$

questions.explanation: A square (100) face has area $a^2=0.16\ \mathrm{nm}^2$. Four corners contribute one atom to the 2D cell and the face centre contributes one more, hence $2/a^2=12.5\ \mathrm{nm}^{-2}$. Counting only corners gives 6.25; counting the entire 3D cell on one face gives 25. Planar density is not volume density.
questions.source: EE3431C Crystal and band theory tutorial.pdf, page 1, Q3; EE3431C Crystal structure part 1.pdf, slide 24

questions.prompt: For a simple-cubic crystal made of identical hard spheres touching along cube edges, which statements are correct?

options.content: The coordination number is 6.
The atomic radius satisfies $R=a/2$.
The conventional cell contains one atom in total.
It has a higher packing factor than FCC.

questions.explanation: Eight corner atoms each contribute $1/8$, giving one atom per cell. Nearest neighbours touch along an edge, so $2R=a$, and each atom has six nearest neighbours. Its packing factor is about 0.52, below FCC's 0.74.
questions.source: EE3431C Crystal structure part 1.pdf, slides 22 and 43

questions.prompt: Which properties belong to a body-centred cubic (BCC) conventional cell?

options.content: It contains two atoms in total.
Its hard-sphere radius is $R=\sqrt{3}a/4$.
Each atom has six nearest neighbours.
The hard spheres touch along cube edges.
Its packing factor equals that of FCC.
Nearest neighbours touch along the body diagonal.

questions.explanation: Corner contributions total one atom and the body-centred atom contributes one more. The contact line is the body diagonal: $4R=\sqrt{3}a$. Face-centred atoms characterize FCC, not BCC. BCC has eight nearest neighbours; six belongs to SC. BCC nearest-neighbour contact is along the body diagonal. BCC packing is about 0.68, not FCC’s 0.74.
questions.source: EE3431C Crystal structure part 1.pdf, slides 23 and 43

questions.prompt: Using the diagram, select the properties of the FCC conventional cell.

image.alt: Oblique projection of a conventional FCC unit cell showing eight distinct blue corner sites and six orange face-centre sites. Shared-site fractions and the effective atom count are not printed.

options.content: The atomic packing factor is approximately 0.74.
Nearest neighbours touch along the cube edge, so $2R=a$.
The coordination number is 12.
The cell contains four atoms after shared-atom contributions are counted.

questions.explanation: The corners contribute one atom and the six face centres contribute three, for four atoms per conventional cell. FCC has 12 nearest neighbours and APF about 0.74. Contact occurs along a face diagonal, giving $4R=\sqrt{2}a$.
questions.source: EE3431C Crystal structure part 1.pdf, slides 24 and 42-43

questions.prompt: Which statements about the diamond crystal structure are correct?

options.content: Its conventional cubic cell contains eight atoms.
It is identical to a monatomic FCC metal because both contain four atoms per cell.
Each atom has four nearest neighbours in a tetrahedral arrangement.
It can be viewed as two interpenetrating FCC sublattices displaced by $(1/4,1/4,1/4)$.

questions.explanation: Diamond uses an FCC lattice with a two-atom basis, equivalently two displaced FCC sublattices. The conventional cell has eight atoms and tetrahedral coordination four; it is not the same as a monatomic FCC structure.

questions.prompt: How does zinc blende differ from the diamond structure?

options.content: The two interpenetrating sublattices are occupied by different atomic species.
GaAs is a zinc-blende compound.
Each atom remains tetrahedrally coordinated to four atoms of the other species.
Its underlying Bravais lattice is BCC.

questions.explanation: Zinc blende preserves the diamond-like geometry but places different elements on the two FCC sublattices. GaAs is a standard example. The underlying Bravais lattice is FCC with a two-atom basis, not BCC.

questions.prompt: A vector in a cubic lattice goes from the origin to the point $(a,2a,-a)$. What is its crystallographic direction?
questions.explanation: Express the vector components in lattice-constant units and reduce to the smallest integers: $(1,2,-1)$. Square brackets denote a direction; parentheses would denote a plane.

questions.prompt: A plane in a cubic lattice intercepts the axes at $a$, $a/2$, and infinity. What are its Miller indices?
questions.explanation: Normalize the intercepts by $a$ to obtain $(1,1/2,\infty)$, take reciprocals to get $(1,2,0)$, and clear any remaining fractions. An infinite intercept gives index zero.

questions.prompt: For first-order X-ray diffraction from planes spaced by $d$, which statements follow from Bragg's law?

options.content: Constructive interference requires $2d \sin(\theta)=\lambda$.
Diffraction works because X-ray wavelengths are many orders of magnitude larger than atomic spacings.
For fixed $d$, increasing $\lambda$ increases the Bragg angle while a solution exists.
A real first-order angle requires $\lambda \le  2d$.

questions.explanation: For $n=1$, Bragg's law is $2d \sin(\theta)=\lambda$. Since $|\sin(\theta)|\le 1$, $\lambda$ cannot exceed $2d$. X-rays are useful because their wavelengths are comparable to interatomic spacings, not vastly larger.
questions.source: EE3431C Crystal structure part 2 XRD.pdf, slides 2-4

questions.prompt: Which statements describe an ideal hexagonal close-packed (HCP) structure?

options.content: Each atom has 12 nearest neighbours.
Close-packed layers follow an ABAB... stacking sequence.
It is one of the three cubic Bravais lattices.
Its packing factor equals that of FCC, approximately 0.74.

questions.explanation: HCP and FCC are both close-packed, so both have coordination 12 and APF about 0.74. HCP uses ABAB stacking and belongs to the hexagonal system, whereas FCC uses ABCABC stacking and is cubic.

questions.prompt: For a cubic binary compound containing $n_A$ atoms of A and $n_B$ atoms of B per cell, its mass density is always $(n_A+n_B)M_A/(N_A a^3)$, even when A and B have different molar masses.

options.content: True
False

questions.explanation: False. Add the masses of both species: $\rho=(n_AM_A+n_BM_B)/(N_A a^3)$. The expression $nM/(N_A a^3)$ applies directly to a monatomic cubic crystal when M is that element's molar mass. Using only $M_A$ incorrectly assigns the same mass to both species.
questions.source: EE3431C Crystal and band theory tutorial.pdf, page 1, Q3; EE3431C Crystal structure part 1.pdf, slides 24 and 27-29
